query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning framework that integrates high-throughput computational data with disorder-sensitive descriptors can predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional DFT or classical MD models.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a multi-principal element disordered solid-solution structure under typical thermal insulation operating conditions.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an ML model trained on high-throughput simulation data and experimental measurements, incorporating descriptors that capture compositional complexity and local lattice distortions.
generation.conditions: The model is applied within the compositional and temperature ranges typical of thermal insulation applications in HEAs, where the disorder is well-characterized and the alloys remain in a stable, single-phase disordered state.
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsic atomic disorder and local lattice distortions that enhance phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: By capturing non-linear relationships between high-dimensional compositional/microstructural descriptors and phonon scattering mechanisms, the ML model more accurately maps the influence of disorder on thermal transport, leading to improved predictions of low thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML framework will achieve at least a 20-30% reduction in prediction error (e.g., mean absolute error) for phonon thermal conductivity compared to predictions from conventional DFT/MD methods, thereby better identifying HEAs with low phonon conductivity.
generation.baseline: Current state-of-the-art predictive methods (standard DFT calculations and classical MD simulations) that do not adequately account for the disorder and configurational complexity of high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be reliable only for HEAs that exhibit significant configurational disorder without substantial local ordering or phase separation; its accuracy may deteriorate for alloys outside the calibrated compositional/temperature range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the prediction improvement is uncertain and may vary depending on the quality and range of high-throughput data available, as well as the choice of disorder-sensitive descriptors.

falsification_experiment.design: Assemble a dataset of high-entropy alloy compositions alongside high-throughput simulation outputs and experimental phonon thermal conductivity measurements under standardized thermal insulation conditions. Run predictions through both the new ML framework and traditional DFT/MD models.
measurements: Quantitative error metrics (e.g., mean absolute error) for each predictive method
Microstructural disorder parameters from experimental characterizations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the ML model does not demonstrably reduce the prediction error (by at least 20%) relative to conventional DFT/MD models, or if no statistically significant correlation is observed between the disorder-sensitive descriptors and the measured phonon thermal conductivity.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available.
